**Checking the three proposed hosts:**

- **Solution 1 (3n+1) fails.** Take the adversarial red-clique partition {v, a₁, b₁}, and {a_i, b_i}, {c_i} for i ≥ 2. Then v's blue neighbourhood has n−1 usable blue matching edges, plus the isolated vertex c₁. Every other vertex has degree 3 < 2n for n ≥ 2, so no blue induced F_n exists. The "compensating pair" step is asserted without justification and is false.

- **Solution 3 (2n+2) fails.** Colour one matching edge v₁w₁ red and everything else blue. The red graph is a single edge, so there is no red induced K₁,₂. A blue induced F_n centred at c₁ or c₂ needs all 2n matching vertices as leaves inducing n disjoint blue edges, but v₁w₁ is missing, so only n−1 edges remain. No other vertex has blue degree ≥ 2n. The "cascading" argument is not carried out, and the counterexample breaks it.

- **Solution 2 (2n+3)** has the most defensible lower-bound idea. Any host on at most 2n+2 vertices has its induced F_n copies sharing an edge, and recolouring that edge red destroys every blue induced F_n while keeping the red graph P₃-free. The upper-bound construction is omitted, so the value is unverified. I did not check it, and I am not certain of the true value.

None of the three is fully justified, and I could not verify any of them completely by hand. Solution 2 is the only one that survives both counterexample checks, so it is the most likely to be correct, though with low confidence.

CHOICE: 2
